review_basis: Original AIP Module 04 site-ready WebP slides individually inspected from three source ZIP archives; lecture describes actual diagram steps, metrics and architectural trade-offs. Renderer verifies R2 originals.
part_title: Responsive AI, Routing, Retrieval and Model Profiling

scenes.title: Build a Responsive AI Experience
scenes.narration: This slide explains three approaches to reduce *perceived* latency. The first panel parallelizes independent work: for example, retrieving from a knowledge base and looking up an authorized API result at the same time. The diagram combines their results only after both are ready. This is useful when the tasks truly do not depend on each other; dependent actions must still run in the correct sequence. The second panel streams model output. Instead of waiting until every token has been generated, the interface displays early tokens while generation continues. Streaming improves the feeling of responsiveness even when the total generation work has not disappeared. In the third panel, the application chooses a latency-optimized inference option when the model and API support it, trading against other workload requirements. Notice the small comparison of standard and optimized response paths. Test time to first token, total duration, accuracy and cost together. The goal is a better user experience, not just a smaller benchmark number.

scenes.title: Route, Trim, and Prioritize
scenes.narration: This slide brings four optimizations into one decision flow. Step one routes the task to a model matched to its difficulty. In the diagram, simple requests use a smaller cost-efficient model, while complex synthesis uses a more capable model. Step two shortens the prompt while retaining necessary instructions. Step three prunes retrieved context: irrelevant or duplicate passages are removed before inference, so the model has fewer distracting tokens. Step four evaluates the whole decision with quality, latency and cost metrics. Follow the circular feedback arrows at the right. A routing policy can be improved after seeing real production outcomes. The example also makes clear that trimming is not unlimited: if an essential policy paragraph or citation is removed, the answer can deteriorate. Optimize around representative user questions and concrete acceptance criteria, and treat model choice, prompt length and retrieval precision as interacting decisions rather than isolated tricks.

scenes.title: Optimize Retrieval Performance
scenes.narration: This slide is a miniature RAG pipeline, and the six numbered steps matter. A user asks a storage-policy question. First, the application normalizes or clarifies the query. Second, it uses the appropriate metadata filters and partitions so it does not retrieve unrelated documents. Third, it can extract important keywords or entities to improve matching. Fourth, hybrid retrieval combines lexical or keyword evidence with semantic vector similarity. Fifth, it reranks candidate chunks and removes irrelevant or duplicate material. Sixth, a generation model answers using the strongest relevant evidence, with citations where appropriate. The lower row reminds us that the search index needs lifecycle management: ingest new information, re-embed changed content, and remove outdated vectors. Finally, the evaluation panel asks whether retrieval actually improved. Check metrics such as recall, precision, grounding quality and latency with real questions. A quick search that returns stale or irrelevant documents is not a successful optimization.

scenes.title: Tune a Model for the Use Case
scenes.narration: Here we compare controlled model settings rather than assuming one default fits every task. At the top left, the temperature slider illustrates the balance between more deterministic and more varied outputs. The nucleus-sampling setting, top-p, narrows or expands the set of probable next tokens. A top-k setting may limit sampling to a fixed number of likely tokens on models that support it. These controls are model-specific and cannot be used identically across every Bedrock model or API. The centre panel runs A and B evaluations using the same representative test prompts, changing one configuration at a time. On the right, a results table compares quality and latency for candidate settings, and the selection panel chooses one that meets requirements. The bottom caution is important: raising or lowering every setting simultaneously makes results hard to interpret. Tune with experiments, measure actual error and response quality, and preserve the approved configuration once you have evidence it works.

scenes.title: Profile the Full FM Request
scenes.narration: This slide asks us to profile the complete foundation-model request, not just model inference. Follow the numbered request timeline from left to right. Preparing and structuring the request consumes time in the application. Retrieving context from a source or knowledge base adds another component. The model invocation itself has latency. Parsing or validating the returned output can take time. Finally, the application collects feedback and traces. The lower timeline separates these stages so we can see where the real bottleneck occurs; the red example highlights a slow model-invocation portion, but a different application could be limited by retrieval or output processing. On the right, the list of useful measurements includes time to first token, end-to-end latency, input and output tokens, error rate and quality scores. Use those components to choose an optimization that addresses the actual delay. Reducing token count is less helpful if a slow external API dominates the user experience.
